findings.explanation: download initially treats the fourth argument as the completion callback, the second as the alternate name, and the third as options (or null when falsy). A function in the second position becomes the callback and clears both name and options. A function in the third position becomes the callback while retaining a string second-position filename. A plain object in the second position is reclassified as options exactly when the third argument is either a function or undefined; that later branch does not alter done, so the callback already normalized from the third position—or initially obtained from the fourth position—remains intact. After normalization and option derivation, download invokes the public this.sendFile method once with fullPath, the derived opts object, and done. It does not start a separate transfer itself.

The attachment name is basename(name || path): a truthy alternate name supplies only the attachment name, while an absent or empty alternate name falls back to the basename of the original path. It never changes the source path. A fresh headers object starts with the generated Content-Disposition. Object.keys copies only own enumerable user-header properties, and lowercasing each key prevents every capitalization of Content-Disposition from replacing the generated value. Object.create(opts) makes the original options object the derived object's prototype rather than copying or mutating it; headers is then an own property pointing to the fresh map. With no options, opts was null, so the derived object has a null prototype. Under the stated plain-data assumptions, neither the caller's options object nor its headers object is mutated here. Public sendFile subsequently writes etag onto this derived child, not the original download options. The inherited-or-own root value controls only this branch: a truthy root preserves path as fullPath, while a falsy or absent root calls resolve(path). No filesystem-containment behavior follows from that handoff.

Public res.sendFile performs its checks synchronously. Missing and empty paths—and other falsy nonstrings—take the required-path error first; a truthy nonstring takes the string-type error. Callback normalization occurs after those checks: a function in the second position becomes done and receives a fresh options object. Otherwise absent/falsy options default to a fresh object, while an ordinary supplied options object is used by identity. A relative string is rejected unless opts.root is truthy; an absolute string passes without root. The path is encoded with encodeURI, the application's enabled('etag') value is assigned over opts.etag, and imported send is called with req, the encoded pathname, and that same opts object. Thus direct sendFile mutates a caller-supplied options object, whereas download passes a derived child and shields its original options. The resulting file stream, response, same opts, and completion closure are handed to the distinct lowercase lexical helper sendfile. None of these synchronous operations is wrapped in callback conversion.

When a callback was supplied, it has unconditional precedence: every helper completion calls done(err), including undefined on success, synthetic directory or abort errors, and original transfer errors. Express then performs no automatic response, next routing, or headersSent check; handling a possibly partial response is the caller's responsibility. Without a callback, EISDIR routes to next() without the error, ECONNABORTED is suppressed, errors whose syscall is write are suppressed, and every other error routes to next(err); successful completion does nothing. Only events delivered through the private helper's callback enter this closure. Invalid-path throws and failures during encoding, application/send setup, or pre-handoff stream creation propagate synchronously and never reach the helper. The sendfile invocation itself also has no try/catch, so a synchronous exception while the helper wires or pipes is not converted into done.

The private sendfile helper registers file listeners in this order: directory, end, error, file, and stream; it then registers response completion through onFinished, conditionally registers headers, and only afterward calls file.pipe(res). Its per-invocation done flag lets the first terminal path win: directory creates a new EISDIR error, abort creates a new ECONNABORTED error, error forwards the original object, and end completes successfully with no argument. Each terminal handler checks done and sets it before invoking the callback, so repeated or callback-reentrant terminal events cannot complete twice. file and stream are state transitions rather than completions. Header-listener installation is decided from options.headers during wiring, but the handler rereads options.headers and runs Object.keys when the headers event occurs, forwarding each then-current own enumerable name/value through res.setHeader. If a terminal failure occurs before any headers event, this helper has not yet applied those custom headers. If headers were already applied, a later failure only follows terminal routing; there is no rollback or header removal.

streaming is initially declared without a value, so it begins undefined; a stream event sets it true and a file event sets it false, with the latest transition governing the deferred check. A response-finish ECONNRESET is converted through onaborted into a new ECONNABORTED error, while another finish error is forwarded unchanged through onerror. If completion already occurred, the delegated guarded handlers no-op for errors and the explicit done check returns for a non-error finish. A non-error finish does not immediately mean success: it schedules a setImmediate check. At that later check, streaming undefined or true causes an abort when not already done; only false proceeds to successful callback completion. An intervening file or stream event can therefore change the result through the latest state. An intervening terminal event sets done and invokes the callback first; both deferred checks then avoid a duplicate. The same guard also collapses multiple deferred finish callbacks to one completion.
